articles.title: Anatomical Connectivity of the Macaque Gaze-following Patch
articles.content: The macaque gaze-following patch (GFP) is a specialized region of the temporal cortex implicated in decoding others' focus of attention and guiding gaze-following behavior. Although the GFP has been characterized functionally, its anatomical connectivity remains largely unknown. To investigate how the GFP is embedded within a putative brain network supporting social interactions, we injected a pair of fluorescence labeled anterograde and retrograde tracers into the GFP of one monkey. Analysis of the resulting material revealed reciprocal connections between the GFP and a region of the inferior parietal lobule, likely corresponding to area PFG, as well as sparse retrograde labeling in the amygdala. In contrast to the expectation that the GFP might be subject to cognitive control signals from the prefrontal cortex, we failed to identify convincing retrograde labeling in prefrontal regions. Overall, this connectivity profile is consistent with a network that translates information derived from others' faces into shifts of attention, while providing little evidence for direct prefrontal control of the GFP.
articles.author: Chong, I.

articles.title: Affective representations and brain-body dynamics during emotional video viewing
articles.content: Emotional events evoke changing neural and bodily responses, but how these responses relate to overall emotional evaluations and how brain and body responses correspond over time remain unclear. Ninety-two participants viewed 25 silent emotional videos, each approximately one minute long, and rated valence and arousal after each video. We recorded brain activity using magnetoencephalography alongside cardiac, electrodermal, respiratory and facial-muscle activity. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) compared source-resolved cortical spectral patterns and peripheral response patterns with participants' valence and arousal ratings, adjusting each affective dimension for the other. Across whole videos, valence similarity corresponded to beta-band power patterns predominantly in left sensorimotor and frontotemporal cortex and to facial-muscle responses. Arousal similarity corresponded to alpha-band power patterns in the right frontoparietal cortex and to phasic electrodermal activity. The neural associations persisted after adjustment for visual and semantic similarities between the videos. Windowed neural correspondence with retrospective valence was significant from around 10 s onwards, with both neural and facial-muscle associations strengthening towards the end of the videos, whereas no significant windowed arousal associations were detected throughout viewing. We further applied dynamic RSA to compare neural and physiological response patterns across videos at different temporal lags. Correspondence exceeded a temporally decoupled reference for facial muscles, heart rate and electrodermal activity, but not respiration rate. On average, corrugator activity preceded corresponding neural patterns by about 1 s, zygomaticus activity occurred at approximately the same time, and heart-rate and electrodermal activity followed about 1.7 s and 4.5 s later, respectively. Together, these findings link overall affective evaluations to complementary neural and peripheral response geometries and reveal signal-specific temporal profiles of ongoing brain-body correspondence.

Network geometry shapes the transformation of task representations across the human cortex
articles.content:

The dimensionality of intrinsic brain connectivity systematically shapes how task representations compress and expand across the cortex, and activity flow modeling shows the active role of network geometry in generating the transformation.

articles.title: Different modes of stimulation at the Neiguan acupoint (PC6) regulate different EEG microstates under VR immersion conditions
articles.content: IntroductionAcupuncture at the Neiguan acupoint (PC6) alleviates postoperative and chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Nevertheless, the central regulatory effects of PC6 stimulation on virtual reality motion sickness (VRMS), a form of physiological vertigo triggered by visual-vestibular sensory conflict, and the corresponding alterations in electroencephalogram (EEG) microstate characteristics remain unclear. Using EEG microstate analysis as the primary approach, this study investigated the effects of different PC6 stimulation modalities on dynamic brain functional changes during VRMS, aiming to further elucidate the potential neural mechanisms underlying acupoint stimulation in VRMS.MethodsParticipants were recruited based on their Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire scores, with a cut-off value of ≥34 used as the inclusion criterion. A total of 200 healthy participants were enrolled and randomly assigned to four equal groups (n = 50 per group): control (32 °C), 40 °C, 44 °C, and 2-Hz transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation (TEAS). The experimental protocol consisted of three phases: baseline, active stimulation, and post-stimulation. All participants received a 40-min stimulation targeting the right PC6 acupoint. EEG data were continuously recorded throughout the experiment.ResultsMicrostate analysis revealed that during the stimulation phase, the 2-Hz TEAS group exhibited significantly increased duration, occurrence, and coverage of microstate D compared with the control group, whereas the 40 °C group affected only the duration of microstate D. During the post-stimulation phase, compared with the control group, the 44 °C group showed a decreased duration of microstate A and significantly increased duration and coverage of microstate B, while the 2-Hz TEAS group continued to exhibit sustained effects on the duration of microstate D.ConclusionThe neuroelectrophysiological signatures of stimulation at PC6 in modulating VRMS are predominantly reflected in the dynamic changes of microstates A, B, and D. Thermal stimulation and low-frequency electrical stimulation engage distinct central modulatory pathways, providing a neuroelectrophysiological basis for optimizing stimulation parameters for in future studies on VRMS.

articles.content: Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used in both research and clinical settings, yet its accuracy can be significantly impacted by subject-specific anatomical anomalies such as brain lesions and skull defects. This study investigates the effects of glioma-related brain lesions and craniotomy-induced bone discontinuities on scalp-recorded EEG signals. articles.title: Endothelin 2-Mediated Neuroinflammation Drives Hypertensive Retinal Dysfunction
articles.content: CONCLUSIONS: Our findings establish endothelin 2 as an important, intraocular pressure-independent contributing factor to hypertension-associated retinal neurodegeneration and identify the endothelin-endothelin receptor type A axis as a potential therapeutic target to prevent vision loss in patients with hypertension.
